output.query: migrainous infarction diagnostic criteria and detection of occult atrial fibrillation after cryptogenic stroke

results.finding: Migrainous infarction (1.4.3) requires an attack typical of previous auras in a patient with migraine with aura, except that one or more aura symptoms persist for more than 60 minutes, with an ischaemic infarct in the relevant area on neuroimaging, and no other diagnosis that better accounts for it. Ischaemic stroke from another cause in a person with migraine is coded as that stroke.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211

results.finding: After cryptogenic stroke, an insertable cardiac monitor detected atrial fibrillation in 8.9% at 6 months and 12.4% at 12 months, against 1.4% and 2.0% with conventional follow-up.
results.source: Sanna T, Diener HC, Passman RS, et al. Cryptogenic stroke and underlying atrial fibrillation (CRYSTAL AF). N Engl J Med 2014;370:2478-2486

output.summary: Migrainous infarction is a diagnosis made only when no other cause explains the infarct; prolonged rhythm monitoring finds occult atrial fibrillation in a minority of cryptogenic strokes that short monitoring misses.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual typical visual aura (5 of 6); the index attack began as her usual aura but left a persistent homonymous hemianopia, so migrainous infarction requires that no other stroke cause be found
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with neurological examination and red-flag review, applying ICHD-3 1.2 and 1.4.3
action_criteria.rationale: The history separates her habitual aura from the index attack and shows that migrainous infarction is provisional until other stroke mechanisms are excluded.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Established 3.5 x 2.5 cm right PCA-territory occipital infarct involving the calcarine cortex; no lesion in another territory; no haemorrhage
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI: define the extent and territory of the occipital infarct and look for infarcts elsewhere
action_criteria.rationale: Required: a persistent hemianopia after an infarct; the size, territory and any other-territory lesions inform the mechanism and the timing of anticoagulation.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal intracranial and neck arteries; right PCA patent; no stenosis, dissection or vasculopathy
action_criteria.label: MR angiography of the intracranial and cervical arteries
action_criteria.rationale: Required in a young ischaemic stroke: excludes large-artery stenosis, dissection and vasculopathy as the mechanism (Kleindorfer DO et al., Stroke 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus anticoagulant negative; normal renal function, blood count, glucose and lipids
action_criteria.label: Blood tests: antiphospholipid antibodies, renal function and blood count before anticoagulation, glucose and lipids
action_criteria.rationale: Recommended: antiphospholipid syndrome is a stroke mechanism in young women and would make a DOAC unsuitable; renal function and blood count are needed to choose and dose the anticoagulant.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Structurally normal heart, normal left atrium and no valve disease; small PFO with Valsalva, no atrial septal aneurysm
action_criteria.label: Transthoracic echocardiogram with agitated saline (bubble) study
action_criteria.rationale: Required in a young ischaemic stroke: looks for a structural cardiac source and a right-to-left shunt, and excludes valve disease that would rule out a DOAC.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: One 43-minute episode of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on day 17, missed by telemetry and the 24-hour Holter
action_criteria.label: Prolonged rhythm monitoring (implantable loop recorder, or at least 30 days) for occult paroxysmal AF
action_criteria.rationale: Required: telemetry and a 24-hour Holter do not exclude paroxysmal AF after an embolic-appearing cortical infarct (CRYSTAL AF; Kleindorfer DO et al., Stroke 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Aspirin is withdrawn once the anticoagulant begins; regular NSAIDs avoided on the DOAC; DOAC unsuitable in antiphospholipid syndrome or pregnancy; triptans contraindicated after the stroke
action_criteria.label: Check the planned DOAC against aspirin, analgesics and her acute migraine treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Required: changing aspirin to a DOAC, choosing acute migraine treatment after a stroke and avoiding NSAID bleeding depend on these interactions.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on migrainous infarction criteria and occult AF detection
action_criteria.label: Optional: literature on migrainous infarction criteria and occult atrial fibrillation
action_criteria.rationale: Background evidence only; not a clinical step in the pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe triptans or ergot derivatives after this ischaemic stroke
Do not continue aspirin alone, or add aspirin to the DOAC, for AF-related stroke prevention
Do not restart combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception
Do not close the PFO: atrial fibrillation explains the stroke and needs anticoagulation in any case
required_recommendations: Revise the diagnosis to cardioembolic right PCA-territory infarct from paroxysmal atrial fibrillation in a woman with migraine with aura; migrainous infarction is excluded because another cause explains the infarct (ICHD-3 1.4.3 D)

Start a DOAC now and stop aspirin when it starts: CHA2DS2-VA is 2 for the stroke (ESC 2024); apixaban 5 mg twice daily (no dose-reduction criterion: age under 80, creatinine 68 umol/L); six weeks after the infarct no further delay is needed
Permanently avoid triptans and ergot derivatives after the ischaemic stroke; treat attacks with paracetamol plus an antiemetic, avoiding regular NSAIDs while on the DOAC

Discuss migraine prevention, which is reasonable now that triptans are contraindicated and NSAIDs are limited (AHS 2021): for example propranolol, amitriptyline or candesartan (only with reliable contraception, as it is contraindicated in pregnancy), with a headache diary
Contraception: no oestrogen-containing method (UKMEC 4 after stroke and with aura); offer a copper IUD or a levonorgestrel IUS, and explain that DOACs must be avoided in pregnancy
Refer for visual rehabilitation (orthoptics or low-vision service, compensatory scanning training) and occupational health for her return to work
Advise her not to drive and to notify the DVLA: a dense homonymous hemianopia does not meet the Group 1 visual field standard

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT adds nothing here: MRI defines the established infarct better and the question is the mechanism, not acute haemorrhage.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated: there is no suspicion of infection, inflammation or subarachnoid haemorrhage.
EEG is not indicated: there has been no seizure and the visual loss is a fixed field defect.

accepted: Cardioembolic right PCA-territory ischaemic stroke occurring during a migraine episode — NOT migrainous infarction; paroxysmal AF identified on implantable loop recorder; switch aspirin to DOAC

differential.key_features: The attack began as her typical aura and the deficit persisted, but ICHD-3 1.4.3 requires that no other cause explains the infarct; paroxysmal AF on the loop recorder does. A large territorial PCA infarct is also less typical of migrainous infarction.
Small shunt only with Valsalva and no atrial septal aneurysm; no known venous thrombosis and no Valsalva at onset; paroxysmal AF provides a stronger mechanism.

differential.diagnosis: Cervical or intracranial artery dissection, or vasculopathy
differential.key_features: No neck pain or trauma; normal intracranial and cervical MRA with a patent right PCA.
Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies negative.

key_clinical_evidence: An infarct during a migraine attack is migrainous infarction only when no other cause explains it (ICHD-3 1.4.3 D)
MRI: established 3.5 x 2.5 cm right PCA-territory infarct with dense left homonymous hemianopia; MRA normal
Implantable loop recorder: 43 minutes of paroxysmal AF on day 17, missed by telemetry and a 24-hour Holter
CHA2DS2-VA 2 after the stroke: a DOAC replaces aspirin
Small PFO without atrial septal aneurysm and negative antiphospholipid antibodies do not compete with AF as the mechanism
Triptans are contraindicated after ischaemic stroke

findings.result: criteria_met refers to her habitual attacks; the index attack is assessed separately below.

12 years of visual aura: an expanding shimmering crescent spreading across one hemifield over several minutes, lasting 20-30 minutes, fully reversible, followed within 30 minutes by a throbbing headache with nausea. About one attack a month.

Began as her typical aura, followed by severe headache, but the left visual field loss did not clear when the aura would have ended and has persisted for 6 weeks (aura symptom persisting over 60 minutes).

Sumatriptan used for attacks until the infarct, then stopped. Aspirin 75 mg daily since discharge. Paracetamol 1 g as needed. Combined oral contraceptive stopped 12 years ago; no current contraception recorded.
No hypertension, diabetes or smoking; BMI 26; no alcohol. Inpatient telemetry and 24-hour Holter in sinus rhythm (outside record).

Dense left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing; visual acuity 6/9 in each eye; pupils and fundi normal. Motor, sensory, reflexes, coordination and gait normal. BP 122/78 mmHg, pulse 74 regular.

Neurological deficit persisting beyond the aura: present. Aura over 60 minutes: present. Systemic symptoms, neoplasia, thunderclap onset, onset after 50, positional or Valsalva trigger, papilloedema, pregnancy and painful eye: absent.

clinical_assessment.impression: Habitual attacks meet ICHD-3 1.2.1 migraine with typical aura (5 of 6 characteristics). The index attack started as her typical aura but left a persistent homonymous field defect; it fits ICHD-3 1.4.3 migrainous infarction only if no other cause explains the infarct (criterion D), so the stroke mechanism has not been established.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met (: 5 of 6 (gradual spread, 5-60 min duration, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min)

alternatives: Warfarin (target INR 2-3) where a DOAC is contraindicated
contraindications: DOACs are not recommended in antiphospholipid syndrome, particularly with triple antibody positivity; warfarin is used instead.
DOACs are not used with a mechanical heart valve or moderate to severe mitral stenosis.
DOACs are avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Triptans (sumatriptan and others) are contraindicated after ischaemic stroke.
interactions: DOAC + aspirin: additive bleeding risk; when a DOAC starts for atrial fibrillation, aspirin is stopped unless there is a separate indication such as recent coronary stenting.
DOAC + NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): increased bleeding, including gastrointestinal; avoid regular use.
DOAC + paracetamol: no clinically relevant interaction.
Apixaban and rivaroxaban + strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors or inducers (azole antifungals, rifampicin, carbamazepine): avoid; none in her current medicines.
apixaban.proposed: Direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, or rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) in place of aspirin 75 mg; paracetamol as needed; sumatriptan previously used
apixaban.summary: Stop aspirin when a DOAC starts unless another indication exists; avoid regular NSAIDs on a DOAC; DOACs are unsuitable in antiphospholipid syndrome and pregnancy; triptans are contraindicated after ischaemic stroke.
warnings: Apixaban dose: 5 mg twice daily; 2.5 mg twice daily only with two of age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 umol/L or more.
Check renal function and full blood count before starting and at least yearly.

metadata.condition_name: Cardioembolic PCA stroke (paroxysmal AF) misdiagnosed as migrainous infarction: loop recorder AF detection, DOAC switch
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: established migraineur with DWI restriction is presumed migrainous infarction; large infarct size and complete hemianopia should raise suspicion; ILR detects PAF missed on initial Holter; DOAC urgently needed

patient.chief_complaint: Infarct on MRI during a headache with visual aura, diagnosed as migrainous infarction; the left visual field defect has not recovered

family_history: Mother has migraine without aura; paternal grandfather had stroke at 70; no family history of AF or coagulopathy

social_history.note: Medical secretary; non-smoker; no alcohol; married; two children (aged 8 and 10); concerned about visual field and return to work

patient.history_present_illness:
A 41-year-old mixed-heritage woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic 6 weeks after an acute hospitalisation. Six weeks ago she presented to the emergency department with a severe headache and left-sided visual disturbance. MRI performed in hospital showed an acute right occipital infarct. She was diagnosed with migrainous infarction and started on aspirin 75 mg and sumatriptan was stopped. She has a 12-year history of migraine with visual aura.

The key problem: she has returned because her visual disturbance has NOT resolved — she now has a persistent left homonymous hemianopia that has been present for 6 weeks. She initially assumed this would improve. She underwent formal visual field testing by an optometrist 2 weeks ago who confirmed a 'dense left homonymous hemianopia.'

On careful re-review of the original episode: she had her typical visual aura (expanding shimmering crescent), but the visual loss persisted after the aura should have resolved.

She has had 12 years of typical migraine with visual aura; this is the first episode with persistent visual deficit. She is not on the combined OCP (appropriately stopped 12 years ago). She has no hypertension; inpatient telemetry and a 24-hour Holter showed sinus rhythm, and she was told she did not have AF. BMI 26. Non-smoker.
